name: bog people

attributes.attribute: bodies lost or drowned in bog lakes, some sacrificed
well preserved by bog water with skin dyed brown
found in 1984, garroted after being fed mistletoe pollen
evidence of human sacrifice and the threefold death

sources: Ross, Anne. “Lindow Man and the Celtic Tradition.” In The Lindow Man: The Body in the Bog, edited by I. M. Stead, J. B. Bourke, and Don Brothwell, 162–169. Ithaca, N.Y.: Cornell University Press, 1986.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Bog people are an archaeological artifact, also called bog men. Across Europe, peat harvesters sometimes meet bodies. These people were lost and drowned in bog lakes. Some were sacrificed in ancient times. Bog water preserves them well. Tannic acid dyes their skin brown. Archaeologists study whether death was accident or rite. Among the sacrificed remains, most come from bogs across Europe. The greatest number come from Denmark. Some finds come from Celtic lands. The Lindow Man was found in 1984 at Lindow near Liverpool. He was garroted after being fed mistletoe pollen. His body shows evidence of human sacrifice and the threefold death.

okr.objective: Describe bog people as preserved bodies from bogs, many from sacrifice.
key_results: Bog people are bodies found by peat harvesters.
Some were lost and drowned, others sacrificed.
Bog water preserves them and tannic acid dyes their skin brown.
The Lindow Man was garroted after being fed mistletoe pollen.
